title: GIFT City Emerges as NRI Magnet With $54 Billion Banking Push
excerpt: Nearly 500 wealthy Indians used the FCNR(B) facility through the GIFT IFSC for the first time — many discovering the financial centre for the first time — and regulators are moving to keep them with bigger investments.
body:
• Nearly 500 high-net-worth NRIs used the FCNR(B) facility through the GIFT IFSC for the first time, with several bringing in an estimated $1-10 million each, IFSCA chairman K Rajaraman told BusinessLine in an exclusive interaction.
  • Twenty international banking units had sanctioned loans aggregating $54.02 billion under the RBI's special swap facility by Aug. 31 — of which $52.82 billion has been disbursed — with sanctions surging from $28.6 billion on Aug. 14 ahead of the deposit window's early closure.
  • The new customers come from established NRI markets (UK, US, Dubai) and new geographies (Mozambique, Mexico); with banks launching wealth-management products at the IFSC, Rajaraman expects many to return with larger investments and use the wider ecosystem for asset management.
  • NRIs can invest in dollars through the IFSC with no INR conversion, no securities transaction tax and unrestricted repatriation — entry points range from IBU deposits (from roughly $500-1,000) to IFSC mutual funds and AIFs (around $150,000), with resident-funded routes capped by the $250,000-per-year LRS limit.

From Mozambique and Mexico to the established NRI markets of the UK, the US and Dubai, a new set of wealthy Indians is streaming into GIFT City in Gandhinagar. Nearly 500 high net-worth individuals have used the foreign currency non-resident (bank) deposit, or FCNR(B), facility through the GIFT International Financial Services Centre for the first time, with several bringing in an estimated $1-10 million each, IFSCA chairman K Rajaraman told BusinessLine.

The significance, Rajaraman said, lies in the reach: many were first-time customers of the GIFT IFSC who had not even been aware of its opportunities.

Twenty international banking units (IBUs) had sanctioned loans aggregating $54.02 billion under the RBI's special swap facility by Aug. 31, of which $52.82 billion has been disbursed — a surge driven by the early closure of the deposit window.

Context & Background

"Twenty international banking units (IBUs) had sanctioned loans aggregating $54.02 billion under the RBI's special swap facility by Aug."

GIFT City — the Gujarat International Finance Tec-City, located between Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar — is India's only operational international financial services centre, conceived in 2015 to draw NRIs, foreign investors and residents seeking overseas options under lighter-touch regulation and moderate taxation. Its IFSC is a special economic zone regulated by the IFSCA, a single unified regulator combining the powers of the RBI, SEBI, PFRDA and IRDAI.

The magnet's core is structural: investments in the IFSC are made in US dollars, so there is no need to convert money into rupees before investing. Financial transactions on the IFSC exchanges are exempt from the securities transaction tax, commodities transaction tax and GST on eligible services, and investors can repatriate both capital and returns without limits. As of late 2025, the centre held almost $30 billion in assets and commitments from 65 jurisdictions and $100 billion in banking assets, according to BusinessLine.

The FCNR(B) leverage was a temporary funding window — an RBI special swap facility that let NRIs channel foreign-currency deposits through the IBUs. Around 33,000 individual bank depositors now hold accounts with IBUs in GIFT City; the 500-odd new retail customers who used the FCNR leverage sit in the higher bracket.

Impact & Analysis

The open question is whether these customers stay beyond the life of the RBI facility. Rajaraman's answer is a deliberate retention strategy: banks are now launching wealth-management products at the IFSC, and he expects many of the new HNIs to return with bigger investments and use the wider ecosystem for their asset-management requirements — turning a temporary funding window into a longer-term customer relationship.

The development also reframes the IFSC's customer map: the FCNR(B) inflow revealed HNI populations in smaller diaspora markets, where the significance lies in the wealth profile, not the headcount.

Caveats remain. Liquidity across the IFSC exchanges is improving but still trails established global markets, and the ecosystem is still developing compared with mature hubs like Singapore and Dubai. For investors, GIFT City is increasingly positioned not as a replacement for those hubs but as an additional India-linked base for capital allocation, fund structuring and succession planning.

Diaspora Angle

This is the diaspora story in its purest form: invest in dollars, skip the INR conversion, avoid the transaction taxes that apply onshore, and repatriate freely. Entry points vary widely: IBU foreign-currency deposits can start from roughly $500-1,000, while IFSC mutual funds offer lower tickets than AIFs, which commonly sit around $150,000 — always confirm the current scheme document, and note that resident-funded routes are capped by the $250,000-per-year LRS limit.

What's Next

The metric to watch is conversion: how many of the roughly 500 new HNIs return with asset-management mandates once the FCNR(B) facility closes. Beyond that, international engagement is accelerating — Singapore's High Commissioner to India highlighted growing Singaporean investment in GIFT City in May 2026, including interest in USD-INR bond issuance. If the new customers stay, GIFT City's next phase moves from funding window to wealth destination.

nri_angle: GIFT City is built for how NRIs handle money: dollar-denominated investing with no INR conversion, no transaction taxes and unrestricted repatriation through a single Indian-regulated financial centre.
